 Social Security’s 3.6% 2027 COLA Increase Could Give Some Retirees a Monthly Raise 2.5X as Large as Others
 Mike Barrington 2026년 11월 19일 목 오후 4:31 UTC 0 (Lane V. Erickson / Shutterstock.com) Quick Read
 Social Security's 3.6% 2027 COLA raises the average retiree's check by about $75 monthly, while maximum-benefit retirees could gain up to $187.
 Because the COLA is a percentage, the largest raise is about 2.5 times the smallest, widening the annual dollar gap by roughly $1,300.
 Rising costs hit smaller checks harder: a hypothetical $50 monthly expense increase consumes about two-thirds of the average raise but only 27% of the largest.

 Inflation sends retirees the bill before Social Security sends the adjustment. Groceries, insurance, and household expenses absorb more income, leaving next year’s benefit increase to help repair purchasing power already lost. That makes the annual cost-of-living adjustment welcome, but it also makes the headline percentage an incomplete guide to anyone’s finances.
 Lane V. Erickson / Shutterstock.com The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% COLA for 2027 this morning, lifting the projected average retirement benefit by $75 monthly. Yet some retirees could receive roughly 2.5 times more under that same adjustment -- the difference comes from the size of the check they already collect.
 The Same Social Security COLA Produces Different Raises
 Social Security applies a percentage adjustment rather than handing every retiree an identical dollar increase. A benefit roughly 2.5 times larger therefore produces a raise roughly 2.5 times larger.
 The SSA’s new 2027 fact sheet projects average retired-worker benefits will rise from $2,095 to $2,170. That replaces the older $2,071 average estimated for January 2026 and provides a better starting point for today’s comparison.
 For perspective, the agency’s 2026 figures included a $4,152 maximum benefit for someone retiring at full retirement age and a $5,181 example for a maximum-earning worker retiring at 70. These reflect particular earnings and claiming assumptions, not amounts everyone can collect.
 Applying 3.6% to those starting amounts illustrates the spread:

 Using these calculations, the largest raise is 2.47 times the smallest -- approximately 2.5 times. The difference reaches $111.10 monthly, or about $1,333 annually. Comparing rounded raises of $187 and $75 instead produces the roughly $1,344 annual gap.

 A Bigger Raise Does Not Guarantee More Buying Power
 Yet, the COLA protects the purchasing power of existing benefits; it does not equalize retirement incomes. As the earlier debate over a larger Social Security adjustment underscored, a bigger increase also reflects the inflation that made it necessary.
 The percentage formula preserves the proportional gap between checks while widening their dollar gap. In the table, the difference between the largest and smallest benefits grows from $3,086 to $3,197.10 monthly.
 That does not establish that the larger-check recipient gains more purchasing power. Their expenses could also be higher. But identical increases in particular bills consume very different shares of each raise.
 Consider a hypothetical $50 monthly increase in household expenses. It absorbs about 66% of the $75.42 adjustment, versus 27% of the $186.52 increase. The smaller-check recipient has $25.42 remaining; the larger-check recipient retains $136.52.
 That helps explain why medical costs can swallow a retirement raise even when the announced percentage sounds encouraging. A uniform adjustment cannot account for each household’s spending mix.
 Key Takeaway
 The useful retirement-planning number is your additional spendable income. Medicare deductions can reduce the deposit, while Social Security’s frozen tax thresholds can expose more benefits to taxation, depending on other income.
 Start with your gross benefit multiplied by 0.036, then compare the estimated increase with changes in premiums, taxes, and recurring bills. Use the personalized SSA notice to finalize your budget..
 A 3.6% COLA delivers equal percentage protection. For retirees stretching smaller checks, though, it delivers fewer dollars to meet the next round of bills.
